O modelo combina, assim, a autonomia de uma startup com a capacidade operacional de uma empresa estabelecida. A ideia é ganhar velocidade e flexibilidade para experimentar, sem precisar construir a estrutura do zero. Segundo o executivo, a proposta também envolve desenvolver uma cultura de experimentação dentro de uma companhia com cinco décadas de atuação no mercado brasileiro. “A ideia da ACE é ser um celeiro de testes para a C&A.” Uma nova avenida de crescimento A transformação da Ace também acompanha uma mudança no posicionamento da marca. De uma linha voltada principalmente a roupas para atividades físicas, ela passou a trabalhar com o conceito de athleisure premium , que combina funcionalidade, conforto e moda para acompanhar diferentes momentos do dia. O movimento ganhou força durante a pandemia, em 2020, quando a procura por roupas esportivas e confortáveis aumentou. Naquele período, a companhia começou a experimentar novos formatos de comercialização, como lojas anexas e operações store in store . A evolução desses testes abriu caminho para a criação de uma unidade de negócios dedicada. Nesse novo posicionamento, a empresa identificou oportunidades em produtos que vão além dos itens tradicionais de treino, como leggings, tops e bermudas. As chamadas terceiras peças, como jaquetas e boleros transpassados, ganharam protagonismo na estratégia. A marca também desenvolveu tecnologias próprias, como o tecido Butter Touch, que combina toque macio e elasticidade. No posicionamento comercial, a Ace aposta no conceito de smart choice : oferecer qualidade comparável à de marcas de referência do segmento premium, com preços entre 20% e 30% abaixo da média dessas concorrentes, de acordo com o executivo. articles.title: “Menos é mais”: a revisão do sortimento pode gerar milhões de reais
articles.titleKo: “Menos é mais”: a revisão do sortimento pode gerar milhões de reais
articles.originalSummary: Conversando com líderes, gestores e especialistas dos segmentos em que atuamos com maior proximidade, há um ponto de convergência entre todos: os próximos anos exigirão muito mais eficiência operacional, disciplina de execução e priorização de esforços das empresas. Especialmente o varejo e as indústrias de bens de consumo têm grandes desafios pela frente. Para citar apenas os mais recorrentes na agenda de todos. Reforma tributária; Nova escala de trabalho; Custo de capital de giro; IA – essa “avalanche” que gera oportunidades, riscos, entusiasmo e receio, simultaneamente e com uma rapidez impressionante. Além destes, gostaria de chamar a atenção para um elemento crítico para as operações de consumo: o sortimento, ou seja, o mix de produtos comercializado. O varejo está buscando cada vez mais melhorar seus resultados, e isso passa certamente por maior assertividade na oferta de produtos e pela eficiência do uso do capital de giro. As indústrias já estão começando a sentir essa demanda de racionalização do varejo e as mais preparadas estão trabalhando em conjunto com seus clientes para definir a melhor solução de produtos para cada loja. Com dados, principalmente os de sell-out por loja, por SKU e de presença nas prateleiras, e o uso de uma boa solução de IA agêntica, é possível definir o mix ideal por loja e buscar a otimização para todos. Racionalizar o sortimento não é um exercício de “eliminar SKUs”, como muitos tratam. As escolhas estão fortemente ligadas à proposta de valor de cada empresa e às suas escolhas estratégicas de como se posicionar junto ao consumidor e de como se diferenciar. Um exemplo muito interessante é o da Costco, nos EUA, que opera com aproximadamente 4 mill SKUs, enquanto seus concorrentes costumam trabalhar com um número muito maior, alguns chegando a 100 mil SKUs. Com essa estratégia, a Costco tem altos volumes e forte capacidade de negociação junto aos seus fornecedores, custos operacionais mais baixos, maior previsibilidade de demanda, baixíssima ruptura, alto giro de mercadorias e forte gestão sobre cada SKU. E os números reforçam a tese de forma irrefutável: Faturamento de USD 270 bi em 2025, crescimento de 8% sobre o ano anterior, em um mercado estável e altamente competitivo como o americano Faturamento SKU: USD: 67,5 MM em 2025, um crescimento também de 8% sobre o ano anterior. É um modelo replicável em todos os formatos e no mercado brasileiro? Certamente não 100%, mas a essência, a lógica, a eficiência e a estratégia podem e devem servir de inspiração para muitos varejistas e indústrias por aqui. Um sortimento inteligente é pensado e executado considerando a combinação da eficiência operacional com a conexão com as missões de compra dos consumidores alvo, facilitando o processo de escolha e gerando a tão desejada eficiência operacional em toda a cadeia, da compra junto ao fornecedor ao produto no carrinho. O sortimento otimizado substitui a lógica de aumentar a variedade e oferecer mais opções de escolha ao consumidor pela de vender mais ao ofertar o que realmente é importante para o shopper e, assim, vender altos volumes. E no caso da sua empresa, a estratégia de sortimento necessita de revisão ou já está totalmente definida e otimizada? Rodrigo Catani é head da Gouvêa Consulting . *Este texto reproduz a opinião do autor e não reflete necessariamente o posicionamento da Mercado&Consumo. Agora, levamos essa expertise para um novo contexto, em que produto, serviço e experiência se encontram na rotina das pessoas”, afirma Marcela Mariano, CMO da Ypê. Enquanto aguardam, os clientes podem utilizar a área de coworking, com wi-fi, ou permanecer no espaço de convivência. A loja também abriga uma cafeteria operada pela rede Café Cultura, especializada em cafés especiais brasileiros, e disponibiliza produtos de cuidados pessoais das marcas Banho a Banho e Flor de Ypê. Novo mercado A abertura marca a entrada da Ypê no segmento de lavanderias de autosserviço. Até então, a presença da companhia no cotidiano dos consumidores estava concentrada principalmente na venda de produtos de limpeza e cuidados pessoais por meio do varejo. “A Lavanderia Tixan Max mostra nossa capacidade de inovar e de encontrar novas formas de estar presente na vida do consumidor, com soluções que fazem sentido para o ritmo das grandes cidades”, destaca Marcela. articles.title: Ornare leva loja de 700 m² à Madison Avenue e amplia presença no mercado americano
articles.titleKo: Ornare leva loja de 700 m² à Madison Avenue e amplia presença no mercado americano
articles.originalSummary: A Ornare vai abrir uma loja de 700 m² na Madison Avenue, em Nova York, no primeiro trimestre de 2027. A unidade será uma das maiores operações da marca brasileira de mobiliário de alto padrão nos Estados Unidos, mercado em que atua há quase 20 anos e mantém 13 lojas . A escolha do endereço coloca a empresa ao lado de algumas das principais marcas internacionais de luxo, em uma região tradicionalmente ocupada por grifes italianas de móveis. A marca brasileira já fornece mobiliário para empreendimentos residenciais de luxo nos Estados Unidos. Em Miami, está presente em todas as unidades do Fendi Château Residences e forneceu closets para o St. Regis Residences Sunny Isles Beach. Em Nova York, participou de projetos de decoração nos edifícios 111 West 57th Street e 35 Hudson Yards. Estrutura para crescer A entrada nesses projetos passa, em boa parte, pelo relacionamento com arquitetos e designers de interiores, profissionais que costumam especificar os fornecedores e influenciar as escolhas dos compradores. “Esses profissionais colocam sua própria reputação em jogo quando recomendam uma marca”, afirma Fabio Aloi, Senior Advisor e membro do conselho da Ornare. Para sustentar o crescimento nos Estados Unidos, Aloi explica que é preciso estabelecer uma estrutura que funcione independentemente da presença dos donos e padronizar as unidades, considerando as diferenças entre as regiões americanas e a necessidade de adaptar a atuação a cada praça. “Os Estados Unidos são como o Brasil: cada estado tem sua característica”, diz. Além dos desafios operacionais, Aloi destaca a diferença de custos em relação aos fabricantes europeus. Enquanto fabricantes de móveis italianos pagam tarifas de 15% em categorias importantes, conforme o acordo comercial entre Estados Unidos e União Europeia, , os produtos brasileiros podem sofrer sobretaxas de até 37,5%, segundo a Abimóvel. articles.title: Fim da escala 6×1: conheça as regras de compensação
articles.titleKo: Fim da escala 6×1: conheça as regras de compensação
articles.originalSummary: O Ministério do Trabalho publicou, nesta segunda-feira, 23, a portaria que estabelece as regras para a implementação do fim da escala de trabalho 6×1 (seis dias de trabalho e um de descanso), cuja primeira etapa entra em vigor em 16 de dezembro. O texto dá um prazo de 90 dias para que os auditores fiscais do trabalho orientem as empresas sobre as novas regras antes de aplicar multas. A portaria confirma dispositivos da emenda constitucional promulgada em outubro pelo Congresso e que foram alvo de flexibilização em liminar concedida pelo ministro Flávio Dino , do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), no âmbito de duas ações movidas por confederações que representam setores empresariais. Segundo a portaria, os trabalhadores terão direito a duas folgas por semana, cada uma com 24 horas consecutivas e uma delas preferencialmente aos domingos. O texto não determina que os dias de descanso sejam seguidos e ressalta que eles não se confundem com o intervalo mínimo entre jornadas previsto na legislação. A portaria diz que acordos ou convenções coletivas poderão estabelecer regimes diferentes de compensação das folgas, desde que seja garantida a média de dois dias de folga por semana dentro do mês. O trabalhador deverá ter pelo menos um dia de descanso após, no máximo, seis dias consecutivos de trabalho. Na decisão de Dino, que ainda precisa ser confirmada pelo plenário do STF, o ministro afastou as travas semanal e mensal do texto constitucional e indicou que os repousos semanais remunerados deveriam ser definidos mediante acordo ou convenção coletiva de trabalho, desde que preservada a integralidade do direito dois descansos semanais remunerados. Quantidade de folgas A portaria do Ministério do Trabalho estabelece que, nos casos de compensação de folgas, o trabalhador deverá ter pelo menos dois dias de descanso por semana, em média, ao longo do mês. Para calcular o mínimo de folgas, o número de dias do mês será dividido por sete e multiplicado por dois, com arredondamento para cima. Na prática, isso significaria oito folgas em fevereiro, nove nos meses de 30 dias e dez nos meses de 31 dias. O texto também proíbe que as férias comecem nos dois dias anteriores a um feriado ou a um dia de descanso semanal, conforme previsto na Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho (CLT). Escalas de revezamento A portaria permite o trabalho aos domingos e feriados nas atividades que precisam funcionar continuamente. Para isso, as empresas deverão organizar escalas de revezamento para garantir o descanso dos trabalhadores. No comércio, ao menos uma folga deverá coincidir com o domingo a cada três semanas. Nas demais atividades, isso deve ocorrer, de preferência, a cada quatro semanas. O trabalho nos dias destinados ao descanso deverá ser pago em dobro, a menos que o trabalhador receba uma folga na mesma semana como compensação. Remuneração e horas extras A portaria estabelece ainda que a redução da jornada, que cairá para 42 horas semanais a partir de 16 de dezembro e para 40 horas semanais um ano depois, não poderá causar diminuição da remuneração dos trabalhadores. O cálculo será feito dividindo o salário mensal por 210 quando a jornada for de 42 horas semanais e por 200 quando cair para 40 horas. A mudança terá reflexos nas horas extras, adicional noturno e outras parcelas calculadas com base no salário-hora. O texto afirma que trabalhadores com diploma de nível superior que recebam pelo menos 2,5 vezes o teto do INSS (R$ 21.1888,88) ficam dispensados das regras de duração do trabalho e do controle da jornada. A portaria também permite que o pagamento das duas folgas seja incorporada ao valor da hora trabalhada, com um acréscimo de 16,667% sobre o salário-hora. Nesse caso, o valor deverá ser discriminado no contracheque, sem redução da remuneração mensal do trabalhador. Além disso, cláusulas de acordos ou convenções coletivas que contrariem os novos limites de jornada e descanso deixarão de produzir efeitos quando as mudanças entrarem em vigor. Banco de horas A

articles.title: Melhor Bocado aposta em franquias e e-commerce para ampliar atuação no B2B e B2C
articles.titleKo: Melhor Bocado aposta em franquias e e-commerce para ampliar atuação no B2B e B2C
articles.originalSummary: A Melhor Bocado, fabricante de donuts, planeja expandir sua atuação no setor alimentício ao ampliar o atendimento B2B a pequenos comerciantes e avançar no mercado B2C por e-commerce e franquias. A principal aposta da marca para o varejo direto ao consumidor é o lançamento da rede de franquias Melhor Bocado Café, que reúne o portfólio completo da empresa. O espaço reúne toda a linha de produtos da empresa e oferece diferentes sabores e finalizações de donuts, croissants, sorvetes e bebidas especiais. Com mais de 38 anos de história, a marca conta atualmente com oito lojas em diferentes pontos da Região Metropolitana de São Paulo. “Vivemos uma transformação importante na alimentação, consumidores mais conscientes buscam equilíbrio, valorizam o bem-estar da saúde física e mental. Com as lojas, acreditamos que podemos ir além da comercialização de donuts”, afirma Hugo Bethlem, CEO da Melhor Bocado. A Melhor Bocado também lançou um e-commerce voltado a pequenos comerciantes, que agora podem comprar os produtos da empresa pelo site. A companhia já atendia esse público por meio de vendedores internos e externos. Para o consumidor final, as compras continuam disponíveis nas lojas Melhor Bocado Café e em pontos de venda parceiros. Novo CEO da rede A Melhor Bocado anunciou Hugo Bethlem, colunista da Mercado&Consumo, como novo CEO da rede. Bethlem já foi vice-presidente do Grupo Pão de Açúcar, onde também esteve à frente de bandeiras como Compre Bem, Sendas e Extra, e teve atuação como senior advisor da Alvarez & Marsal Performance. Sua experiência inclui ainda passagens por empresas como Carrefour, Hopi Hari, Sé Supermercados e Dicico. Com mais de quatro décadas de experiência em posições de liderança, especialmente no varejo, o executivo é cofundador do Capitalismo Consciente Brasil e atualmente preside o conselho da organização. articles.title: Miss Make entra no e-commerce e amplia alcance para além das 63 lojas
articles.titleKo: Miss Make entra no e-commerce e amplia alcance para além das 63 lojas
articles.originalSummary: Com 63 lojas espalhadas pelo País, a Miss Make, rede goiana de maquiagem, entrou no comércio eletrônico com o lançamento de sua loja virtual. Com a operação online, a marca passa a atender consumidores de cidades onde ainda não mantém lojas físicas. O e-commerce reúne produtos de maquiagem, cuidados com a pele e os cabelos e acessórios de marcas nacionais e importadas. A marca prevê ampliar o catálogo nos próximos meses. “A Miss Make nasceu do sonho de fazer toda mulher se sentir mais poderosa, com produto bom e preço justo. A loja online leva isso para quem ainda não tem uma Miss Make na sua cidade”, afirma Misnay Assis, fundadora da marca. Desde a fundação, em 2020, a empresa concentrava as vendas nas unidades físicas, distribuídas entre pontos de rua, shopping centers e quiosques. O lançamento da loja online foi apresentado em uma live conduzida por Misnay, transmitida simultaneamente pelo YouTube, Instagram e TikTok. Vendas online avançam no Brasil A iniciativa da Miss Make acompanha o crescimento do comércio eletrônico no Brasil. O setor faturou R$ 125 bilhões no primeiro semestre de 2026, segundo dados da Associação Brasileira de Inteligência Artificial e E-commerce ( Abiacom ). O resultado representa uma alta de 24,37% em relação aos R$ 100,5 bilhões registrados no mesmo período de 2025. Nos seis primeiros meses do ano, foram contabilizados 242 milhões de pedidos, com ticket médio de R$ 517. A expectativa da entidade é encerrar 2026 com 460,87 milhões de pedidos e faturamento acima de R$ 260 bilhões. As estratégias de comunicação também ganharam espaço no setor, com lojistas ampliando o uso de conteúdos para redes sociais, vídeos, transmissões ao vivo e parcerias com influenciadores para atrair consumidores e gerar vendas. A Abiacom espera que o ritmo de crescimento seja mantido no segundo semestre, com avanço da digitalização do consumo, das plataformas de vendas e do uso de Inteligência Artificial na experiência de compra. articles.title: Alles Alimentos entra no foodservice com marca própria e 20 produtos
articles.titleKo: Alles Alimentos entra no foodservice com marca própria e 20 produtos
articles.originalSummary: A Alles Alimentos lançou a marca Fortena, voltada ao mercado de foodservice . Com um portfólio de 20 produtos, a linha é direcionada a restaurantes, lanchonetes e cozinhas industriais para otimizar o tempo de preparo, padronizar receitas e controlar custos operacionais. A marca chega com um portfólio que inclui almôndegas, bacon, linguiça tipo calabresa, carne moída, peito de frango desfiado, pernil desfiado, cupim desfiado, costela desfiada e uma opção desfiada sabor carne seca. No segmento de hamburguerias, a empresa apresenta quatro versões de hambúrguer: bovino smash, de 90 gramas; bovino tradicional, de 90, 120 e 150 gramas; bovino sabor picanha, de 90 e 120 gramas; e misto de carnes bovina e suína, com 56 gramas. Hambúrgueres para diferentes operações Entre os destaques do portfólio está a linha de hambúrgueres. O smash foi desenvolvido para facilitar a prensagem na chapa, enquanto o tradicional é oferecido em diferentes gramaturas, destinadas a atender desde lanchonetes de alto giro até restaurantes que servem sanduíches maiores. O hambúrguer sabor picanha apresenta caramelização uniforme e baixa retração durante o preparo, de acordo com testes realizados pela marca. A versão mista, de menor gramatura, foi desenvolvida para o preparo de sanduíches simples ou duplos. Os produtos também foram avaliados após 30 minutos em condições simuladas de delivery . Linha reúne almôndegas e linguiças calabresas A linha inclui almôndegas bovinas e mistas, elaboradas com carnes bovina e suína, em embalagens de 1 quilo. Os produtos são moldados e ultracongelados antes de chegar ao consumidor, prontos para o preparo. Já as linguiças tipo calabresa são comercializadas em três formatos: reta e curvada, ambas em embalagens de 2,5 quilos, e fatiada, de 1 quilo. Os produtos passam por cozimento e têm sabor defumado. A marca também oferece bacon cozido e defumado, produzido a partir de barriga suína e disponível em fatias ou cubos. Comercializadas em embalagens de 1 kg, as duas versões podem ser utilizadas em hambúrgueres, massas, risotos, molhos e recheios. A linha de carnes temperadas, cozidas, desfiadas e congeladas é comercializada em embalagens de 1 kg. A seleção inclui ainda carne moída bovina congelada, com teor de gordura de até 9%, comercializada em embalagens de 1 kg. articles.title: Bahama Buck’s Hosting Annual Free Sno Day on December 1
articles.titleKo: Bahama Buck’s Hosting Annual Free Sno Day on December 1
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Bahama Buck’s Franchise Corporation will celebrate the 20th anniversary of its annual Free Sno Day on Tuesday, December 1, inviting guests at participating locations nationwide to enjoy a complimentary Sno (up to 12 oz.) as the brand kicks off the holiday season. The longstanding holiday tradition has grown into a nationwide community event. In 2025, Bahama Buck’s participating shops distributed 68,843 free Sno products, representing an estimated retail value of approximately $316,000 in product value, across 106 locations. The 2026 celebration is expected to bring together a similar number of participating shops, continuing a tradition that has become a meaningful part of the holiday season for guests and franchise communities. For some families, Free Sno Day marks the official beginning of the holidays. “One family in Lubbock, TX recently shared that Free Sno Day is how they kick off the holiday season every year. They shared, ‘The holidays can’t start without Free Sno Day!’ Stories like that remind us why this tradition means so much to our Bahama Buck’s family,” said Blake Buchanan, founder and CEO of Bahama Buck’s Franchise Corporation. “Celebrating 20 years of Free Sno Day is a special milestone. What started as a way to give back has become a tradition that brings communities together and helps us Bless our Guests in a meaningful way. We’re grateful to everyone who has made Free Sno Day part of their holiday season.” Guests are invited to visit participating Bahama Buck’s locations on Tuesday, December 1, to enjoy a free Sno and celebrate two decades of this holiday tradition. articles.title: Wendy’s Launches its First Merch Store
articles.titleKo: Wendy’s Launches its First Merch Store
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . The Wendy's Shop is officially open for business. Your go-to spot for fresh, never-frozen beef* is taking its quality commitment to the next level by giving fans a fresh new way to check off their gift lists. This holiday season, Wendy’s launched its first-ever merch store, featuring collections that turn what fans already love about Wendy’s into wearable, giftable and collectible keepsakes. From full fits to festive stocking stuffers, the Wendy’s Shop has something for every occasion and budget. The Vintage Collection: Inspired by the same iconic brand fandom behind the recent return of Wendy’s yellow packaging, the Vintage Collection goes old school with pieces featuring nods to past uniforms, packaging and other design details from Wendy’s history. The Core Collection: For fans who like their Wendy’s with a bit of a modern twist, the Core Collection puts a fresh spin on everyday essentials, including hats, hoodies and tees inspired by Wendy’s Frosty, Hot n’ Crispy Fries and more. The shop’s offerings go well beyond items you can wear. Fans can also deck the halls with a Frosty-themed ornament and snag retro-inspired stocking stuffers, giving them even more ways to bring a little Wendy’s into their everyday lifestyle. articles.title: Parceria entre McDonald’s e MBRF leva chester ao fast-food neste Natal
articles.titleKo: Parceria entre McDonald’s e MBRF leva chester ao fast-food neste Natal
articles.originalSummary: O McDonald’s vai incluir o Chester Perdigão em seu cardápio brasileiro pela primeira vez. A novidade é resultado de uma parceria com a MBRF e marca a entrada de uma das proteínas mais tradicionais das ceias de Natal em uma nova ocasião de consumo ao longo do mês de dezembro. Batizado de Chester Club, o sanduíche começa a ser vendido em 8 de dezembro, em mais de 1,2 mil restaurantes da rede no Brasil. O lançamento foi anunciado nesta segunda-feira, 23, durante um encontro da MBRF com jornalistas, em São Paulo, para apresentar a campanha de Natal da companhia. O produto combina pão de batata, cebola crispy, queijo emmental, bacon, Chester Perdigão e geleia defumada. O sanduíche também será oferecido em um combo com batatas fritas e bebida. Segundo Ilca Sierra, diretora de Marketing do McDonald’s no Brasil, a parceria procura aproveitar a presença do Chester na memória afetiva dos brasileiros e estender a experiência natalina a outros momentos de consumo. “A nossa intenção aqui justamente foi unir essa tradição enorme com essa inovação”, afirmou. A executiva destacou que o Natal envolve uma série de encontros e atividades que acontecem antes da ceia, como as compras de presentes nos shoppings e as confraternizações entre amigos e familiares. A proposta do Chester Club é participar desses momentos, segundo ela, oferecendo uma opção sazonal associada aos sabores da data. MBRF amplia ocasiões de consumo do Chester Para a MBRF, que é a fornecedora oficial dos Arcos Dourados no Brasil e países da América Latina, a parceria representa uma oportunidade de levar o Chester a consumidores que não necessariamente comprariam uma ave inteira para preparar em casa. Manoel Martins, vice-presidente de Mercado Brasil e Marketing da companhia, comemorou a chegada da proteína ao cardápio da rede. “Nós estamos levando o Chester também para a hora do lanche, para outra ocasião de consumo”, afirmou. Durante o evento, os executivos informaram que a parceria para desenvolver o sanduíche vinha sendo trabalhada havia bastante tempo. O Chester Club será uma edição limitada, com comercialização prevista para o período natalino. A companhia não divulgou estimativas de volume de vendas nem detalhes sobre a participação esperada do produto no faturamento da rede. articles.title: Kura Sushi Proves Revolving Sushi Can Work Anywhere in America
articles.titleKo: Kura Sushi Proves Revolving Sushi Can Work Anywhere in America
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Kura Sushi entered the U.S. in 2008. Kura Sushi USA is close to opening its 100th U.S. unit in December, and the biggest lesson from this growth, according to CEO Jimmy Uba, is that there really isn’t anywhere in America that isn’t excited about revolving sushi. To his point, the Japanese-born company has emphasized growth outside of the top 25-30 DMAs in recent years, including openings in Glen Allen, Virginia, and West Des Moines, Iowa. A New spot iGainesville, Florida is scheduled to open next month. These sub-top 30 markets have performed just as well as the larger cities, Uba says. “It’s really been phenomenal to realize just how eager America is for revolving sushi and sushi broadly,” Uba says. But this demand wasn’t always so obvious. Kura was founded in 1977 in Sakai, Osaka, Japan, by Kunihiko Tanaka. The brand ventured into the U.S. in 2008. By then, there were already over 150 units in Japan; however, the first U.S. iteration wasn’t revolving sushi with the tech-forward conveyor belts. It was actually a traditional sushi restaurant. “Even with that established category [in Japan], when we first came to the United States, we just assumed that nobody would be interested in it,” Uba says. It wasn’t until a year later that the company decided to pivot to its well-known revolving model. Then the company went public in 2019. And as it turns out, Americans couldn’t get enough of it. Restaurants in smaller DMAs are hitting system AUVs, and if they’re not doing that, they’re hitting system cash-on-cash returns, which is Kura’s primary “go or no go” deciding factor when picking a site. Uba says these secondary/tertiary locations tend to be inside malls where they are the main attraction. “As long as you’re in there, you have a captive audience,” Uba says. “So you might not have the same density as you would in say L.A., for example, but you have a really wide draw, and so that’s been working out very well for us.” Kura’s long-term goal is 300 U.S. units. The company hasn’t set a formal timeline or date to hit that benchmark, but one can do the math. The chain expects to open 17 restaurants in fiscal 2027, 18 in 2028, and 19 in 2029. At that pace, the company should reach the 300-unit mark in about a decade. But Uba wants to make it clear that Kura’s focus isn’t just growth for the sake of it. The bigger North Star is sustaining strong unit-level economics. That’s why the brand doesn’t want to be held to a certain timeframe; it wants flexibility in how it will get there, ensuring that it remains profitable on the way to the top. The expansion comes with uniqueness. Kura doesn’t have any prototypes. Every single restaurant is built to match the location, and that’s a deliberate decision. The company wants to be open to any and all opportunities, and doesn’t want a strict prototype preventing it from entering certain real estate, Uba explains. But on the flip side, that also means the chain doesn’t expect meaningful savings in buildout costs; costs are expected to rise from $2.4 million to $2.6 million, and that’s mostly because of tariffs on buildout materials. If tariffs were to go away, Kura would likely see around $100,000 in savings. “We’re really proud that we’ve been able to maintain our cash-on-cash returns of about 33 percent in spite of elevated buildout costs, and I think we’ve done a really good job in terms of just trying to find little cost-saving opportunities and add those up to sustain our unit-level economics,” Uba says. In terms of construction timelines, Kura has gone from 180 to 150 days over the past three years. articles.originalSummary: Com crescimento de 50% nas vendas de produtos internacionais em 2026, a Amazon acrescentou mais de 4 milhões de itens importados dos Estados Unidos e da Ásia em 2026, com destaques para livros físicos, vestuário, discos de vinil e utensílios para casa. A oferta internacional complementa os produtos brasileiros disponíveis em mais de 50 categorias, comercializados também por milhares de vendedores locais. “Nosso objetivo é sempre oferecer mais produtos, com preços competitivos e entrega rápida, gerando conveniência para todos os brasileiros. Isso está em linha com o desejo crescente dos consumidores brasileiros por novidades”, afirma Hayley Muller, líder de seleção internacional da Amazon Brasil. Logística e custos de importação Desde a chegada da seleção internacional ao Brasil, em 2024, a Amazon reduziu os prazos de entrega em cerca de 40%. Nos últimos 12 meses, a promessa de entrega ficou 22% mais rápida, com pedidos destinados a São Paulo chegando em até sete dias. As condições de compra também incluem opções de pagamento utilizadas no mercado brasileiro, como Pix e parcelamento. Para produtos vendidos e entregues pela Amazon, os preços são apresentados em reais e incluem impostos e custos de importação. Já nas compras feitas de vendedores internacionais, a plataforma informa uma estimativa dos tributos e das taxas antes da conclusão do pedido. Os itens contam com a Garantia de A a Z, quando aplicável, que prevê suporte ao consumidor em situações como recebimento de produtos danificados, com defeito ou diferentes da descrição, com possibilidade de reembolso ou substituição. articles.title: Snooze Eatery Unveils Holiday Menu Featuring Ube Pancakes and Returning Favorites
articles.titleKo: Snooze Eatery Unveils Holiday Menu Featuring Ube Pancakes and Returning Favorites
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . The new holiday menu will be available at Snooze locations nationwide. Seasonal offerings will be available for a limited time through Feb. 2. Purple pancakes, unexpected coffee creations and the return of a highly requested breakfast favorite. Snooze Eatery is shaking up the holiday breakfast scene with a bold new menu launching nationwide Nov. 27. From introducing the rich flavors of ube to bringing the fan-favorite Habanero Pork Belly Benny back to the menu, the Denver-born restaurant is proving there’s always room to push the boundaries of breakfast. Leading the menu are the purple Ube Pancakes, featuring fluffy ube buttermilk pancakes studded with white chocolate chips, layered with blueberry coulis, fresh blueberries and toasted coconut, crowned with a cloud of ube whipped cream. With its bright purple color and subtly sweet, nutty flavor, ube is an unexpected ingredient that Snooze makes approachable through familiar breakfast favorites. The Ube Latte brings the same energy to the coffee cup, blending rich espresso with house-made vanilla ube syrup and guests’ choice of milk. For those who wake up on the savory side, Snooze is bringing back the Habanero Pork Belly Benny. This anything-but-ordinary Benedict piles braised habanero pork belly, bacon-espresso jam, poached cage-free eggs and house-made cream cheese hollandaise onto an English muffin. With the perfect balance of heat, sweetness and savory richness, this bold brunch favorite is back, giving guests something to crave this holiday season. The holiday indulgence doesn’t stop at the plate. Snooze is bringing festive flavors to its beverage lineup with two seasonal creations: The Pistachio Mint Latte blends rich espresso with pistachio and mint syrups for a festive twist on a coffeehouse favorite, while the Pistachio Mint Matcha combines earthy matcha with the same sweet, refreshing flavors. Both are available hot or iced with guests’ choice of milk, with iced versions topped with velvety vanilla cold foam. Also joining the permanent beverage menu is the Carajillo, a classic espresso cocktail made with espresso and Licor 43. Snooze puts its own spin on the cocktail with the addition of vanilla syrup, creating a rich, aromatic sip that brings a little extra sweetness to the brunch table. For guests looking to make their favorite beverages their own, Snooze is introducing two additional customization options: Vanilla Cold Foam, a smooth, creamy topping that can be added to any beverage, and Protein Bump, which adds 7 grams of protein. “At Snooze, we’ve always believed breakfast should be anything but ordinary,” said Stacy Moss, chief marketing officer at Snooze Eatery. “We love taking familiar favorites and giving them an unexpected twist, while introducing guests to flavors they may not have experienced before. This menu is a great example of that balance, bringing something new and exciting to the table alongside a fan favorite our guests have been asking us to bring back.” The new holiday menu will be available at Snooze locations nationwide. Seasonal offerings will be available for a limited time through Feb. 2, while the Carajillo will remain on the menu permanently. For more information, visit snoozeeatery.com or follow Snooze on Instagram at @eatsnooze. Download the Snooze app to join MySnooze Bennyfits and start earning Jacks with every visit to redeem for free pancakes, sides, beverages and more. The St. Anthony, a Luxury Collection Hotel and AAA Four Diamond historic property located in the heart of downtown San Antonio has promoted Executive Chef Leo Davila to Culinary Director, expanding his leadership across the hotel’s diverse dining and culinary experiences. In his new role, Chef Leo will lead the direction of the hotel’s culinary identity, aligning the dining experience across its restaurants including Esencia, Anacacho Coffee & Cantina, Gallery On the Park, The St. Anthony Club, in-room dining, poolside offerings and special activations under a unified vision that elevates the guest experience while honoring each venue’s distinct character. His leadership will extend to championing culinary excellence through a commitment to operational performance, exceptional quality standards and the continued development of the hotel’s culinary talent.Executive Chef Jarrod will continue to oversee hotel food and beverage operations, with a focus on banquets, catering, weddings and special events. “Chef Leo’s promotion is an exciting next chapter for our culinary program at The St. Anthony,” said Maria Martinez, General Manager of The St. Anthony Hotel. “What makes Chef Leo so special is not only his incredible creativity and talent, but also the genuine passion and heart he brings to everything he does. His love for San Antonio, its culture, and culinary traditions is reflected in every dish he creates. I am incredibly proud to see him take on this expanded role, bringing his vision and passion to every corner of our property while ensuring each of our dining experiences maintains its own unique identity.” Chef Leo brings a deep understanding of the city’s culinary heritage to his work. He has developed a distinctive style that blends sweet and savory elements, creating a vibrant fusion of both cuisines. His innovative approach to San Antonio regional fare has earned widespread recognition, including a 2026 James Beard Award semi-finalist nomination for Anacacho Coffee & Cantina, becoming a Food Network Chef alumnus, ranking #17 on the San Antonio Express-News’ Top 50 Restaurants in 2026, and securing a spot on Texas Monthly’s Top 25 Best Taquerias list. Leo has served as a Chef Ambassador for San Antonio’s UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy designation, representing the city on a global stage. In spring 2024, he traveled to Shunde, China, participating in a Guinness World Record event while showcasing San Antonio cuisine to more than 1,000 festival attendees. “I’m proud to be from San Antonio, and it’s special to have the opportunity to continue building something meaningful in a hotel with such a rich history,” said Chef Leo Davila. “I look forward to bringing my perspective to every corner of the property while celebrating the city’s culinary identity and creating memorable, storytelling experiences for our guests.” To learn more, please visit www.thestanthonyhotel.com or follow along on @TheStAnthonyHotel. With more than two decades of restaurant development experience spanning real estate, design, construction, and franchise growth, Peter Busse has built his career around bringing brands to life and creating development strategies designed for long-term success. Now, as Chief Development Officer of Checkers & Rally’s, Busse is bringing that experience to one of the quick-service industry’s most recognizable drive-thru brands at a pivotal point in its evolution. In his role, he oversees development across the system, including new unit growth, acquisitions, remodels, real estate strategy, design and construction, with a focus on strengthening restaurant economics, supporting franchisees and positioning the brand for sustainable expansion. Prior to joining Checkers & Rally’s, Busse led development for Torchy’s Tacos, overseeing real estate, design, construction and facilities while helping guide the brand’s nationwide expansion. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade with Yum! Brands, where his roles included supporting franchise development across Africa and leading corporate construction for Taco Bell. Throughout his career, Busse has developed a leadership philosophy rooted in accountability, collaboration and respect, values he first began learning in his earliest days in the workforce. As he steps into his newest chapter with Checkers & Rally’s, he is focused on building strong teams, partnering closely with franchisees and creating restaurants that stand out in an increasingly competitive marketplace. What was your first job? My first job was as an assistant store planner and designer for a boutique supermarket group. Because each location had its own character, I had the opportunity to create individual designs rather than simply replicate a standard prototype. That experience is where I first discovered my passion for bringing brands to life through design and development. It also taught me the value of hard work, personal accountability, attention to detail, and treating everyone with respect. What’s your favorite menu item at Checkers/Rally’s? The Big Buford. It’s bold, iconic, and represents so much of what the brand was built on, so it quickly became my go-to. That said, I also have a weakness for the Funnel Cake Fries. Favorite cuisine beyond Checkers/Rally’s? Indian and Thai—anything with bold flavors and a little heat. Having grown up in South Africa and lived and worked in different parts of the world, I’ve always enjoyed experiencing different cultures through food. I particularly love dishes that are meant to be shared and bring people together—and a little spice never hurts. Who inspires your leadership? I don’t draw inspiration from just one person. articles.title: Bad Ass Coffee of Hawaii and the Potential of ‘Connected Data’
articles.titleKo: Bad Ass Coffee of Hawaii and the Potential of ‘Connected Data’
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Bad Ass Coffee continues to expand its national footprint. Bad Ass Coffee of Hawaii has a story that travels well. Its name, Tom Wylie explained in an episode of QSR Uncut, pays tribute to the donkeys that carried heavy loads of coffee beans down Hawaii’s mountains. Stores aim to bring a sense of experience and place to guests, whether they’re on vacation or stopping in for a regular drink. But as the brand grows, Wylie says, a compelling story needs to be supported by a strong business model. That means giving franchisees tools to manage costs, understand customers, and act on information without getting buried. Wylie and Diane Le, who leads marketing for PAR Technology’s restaurant division, discussed what connected data unlocks for operators. 1. The best data is useful while there’s still time to act Restaurants operate on thin margins, and Wylie says waiting for financial statements can leave sore leaders responding to problems weeks after they began. His example: By the time a monthly period ends and financials arrive, an issue that started early in the period may have been affecting the business for 45 days already. A labor or inventory problem discovered then has compounded. Connected systems offer a timelier view of what’s happening across sales, labor, and inventory. Wylie cautions against overreacting to every fluctuation, but says a weekly look at the right numbers uncovers when something needs attention. For him, the goal isn’t an endless dashboard. Rather, he’s looking for a small set of meaningful KPIs that help an operator assess a store’s health and decide where to investigate. The wisdom: Collect information to support decisions, not just reports. The sooner an operator can see a problem, the sooner they can respond. 2. Connected data should tell one clear story Most restaurant operators depend on multiple systems: point of sale, back-office operations, and loyalty, among others. The challenge is making sure systems understand one another. Wylie recalls Bad Ass Coffee’s earlier infrastructure could be connected, but the process required effort and information didn’t line up cleanly. One system might use a different unit of measure than another, making it harder to understand, say, inventory and costs. Le describes “connected data” as more than putting information on one screen. It means ensuring the underlying information, such as a transaction, a guest, a menu item, or a recipe, can be understood across systems. That can reduce the work of reconciling conflicting information and help operators see how different parts of the business relate. A loyalty promotion, for example, isn’t just a marketing event; it can also affect what a store needs to have on hand and how it plans labor. The wisdom: Ask not only whether your systems can connect, but whether the information flowing between them is consistent enough to guide a decision. 3. Build your technology around how the business actually operates A system that works well for one restaurant concept won’t necessarily fit another without adjustment. At Bad Ass Coffee, Wylie says, the range of ingredients, syrups, and drink combinations made an off-the-shelf approach difficult to manage. As the brand began rolling out PAR’s point-of-sale system, the team configured it around Bad Ass Coffee’s products and recipes. Wylie said four to six stores were currently active on the system. The intent is to make sales and recipe information useful for understanding inventory. If a store sells a certain number of lattes, the system can help establish how much coffee and syrup should have been used. An inventory variance then gives an operator a reason to look closer. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Holiday magic shouldn’t come with a side of kitchen stress. This year, Golden Corral is giving guests more time to relax with loved ones, offering craveable favorites and convenient meals built to share at home. Guests can now skip the kitchen and go straight to the feast, with Golden Corral’s Holiday Buffet including several tried-and-true holiday favorites, including: Holiday Entrées: Roasted Turkey, Holiday Glazed Ham, and Bone-In Pork Roast Classic Sides: Mashed Potatoes, Gravy, Sweet Potato Casserole, Homestyle Stuffing, Sweet Corn Pudding, Green Bean Casserole, and Cranberry Sauce Fresh-Baked: A dozen Golden Corral Yeast Rolls and a choice of a whole Pumpkin or Pecan Pie And because there’s always room for something new: NEW! 5-Cheese White Mac & Cheese: An extra helping of creamy, cheesy comfort NEW! Cookie Butter Cheesecake: A sweet dessert-bar addition featuring the warm, spiced flavor of cookie butter “When we think about the holidays at Golden Corral, we think big: big plates, lots of variety, and plenty to dig into,” said Darryl Mickler, Senior Vice President of Food & Beverage at Golden Corral. “This year, we’re having a little fun with the menu, from our new 5-Cheese White Mac & Cheese to the warm, spiced flavors of Cookie Butter across our new desserts and beverages. Whether it’s new items or traditional holiday favorites, there’s something for everyone.” For guests celebrating at home, Golden Corral Holiday Meals To Go make it simple to serve a full meal without the prep hassle. Family-size meals serve six to eight people and include a choice of Roasted Turkey, Holiday Glazed Ham, or Bone-In Pork Roast, plus mashed potatoes, gravy, stuffing, choice of vegetable, cranberry sauce, a dozen yeast rolls, and a whole Pumpkin or Pecan Pie. Guests can choose from ready-to-eat or Heat & Serve options, as well as Turkey Breast, Pork Roast, and Ham Sliced Meals. Sliced Meals include a choice of Sliced Ham, Sliced Turkey, or Sliced Pork Roast with two side choices, Yeast Rolls, and cookies. Meals To Go are available for pickup or delivery through GoldenCorral.com or the Golden Corral App. The last day to order Thanksgiving meals is Nov. 23, and the last day to order Christmas Eve meals is Dec. 21.* For a sweet sip to pair with the spread, Golden Corral is introducing three NEW Cookie Butter beverages: Cookie Butter Tea, Cookie Butter Cola, and Cookie Butter Hot Coffee. Available Nov. 2 through Jan. 3, the beverages join the NEW Cookie Butter Cheesecake for a limited-time lineup made for the coziest time of year. Golden Corral is also making gifting a little more rewarding with its annual holiday gift card promotion. Now through Jan. 3, 2027, guests who purchase $50 in gift cards in-restaurant, through GoldenCorral.com or the Golden Corral App will receive a $10 Bonus Card. Purchases must be made in $50 increments to quality for additional Bonus Cards, which are redeemable Jan 4 through Feb. 11, 2027.** Whether guests dine in or take the feast home, Golden Corral is giving families one less thing to worry about this season — so they can spend less time cooking and more time with the people who make the holidays special. For more information or to check out local restaurant hours, visit GoldenCorral.com. The Holiday Buffet is available for a limited-time, after 4 p.m. Monday-Friday. Weekend hours, items, and availability may vary. *Orders must be placed at least 72 hours in advance. Meals are not available through third-party delivery apps. Pricing and availability may vary by location. **Gift cards purchased through third-party retailers are not eligible. articles.title: Popmenu Study: Nearly Half of Americans Plan to Order Thanksgiving Takeout or Delivery in 2026
articles.titleKo: Popmenu Study: Nearly Half of Americans Plan to Order Thanksgiving Takeout or Delivery in 2026
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Outsourcing all or part of Thanksgiving dinner remains a popular choice for households across the U.S. Nearly half (47%) of consumers plan to order takeout or delivery for Thanksgiving this year, a dip from 53% last year, but well above 37% reported in 2024 and 32% in 2023. Another 5% expect to dine in person at a restaurant, on par with last year. The findings come from a nationwide November 2026 survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers by Popmenu, a restaurant tech firm that works with 12,000+ restaurants. The study also looks at how rising food prices are changing what families put on the Thanksgiving table. How much are consumers spending on Thanksgiving dinner? Whether ordering out or cooking at home, the vast majority (86%) of consumers think the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is out of control; 62% plan to spend less on Thanksgiving this year compared to last year as they work to stay within budget. On average, consumers hosting Thanksgiving estimate they will spend ~$200 on dinner this year—half are serving 6 to 10 people. How are consumers making Thanksgiving more affordable? Whether they’re hosting or joining holiday festivities as guests, consumers are taking various measures to manage costs: 42% – Celebrating the holiday with fewer people 31% – Buying less expensive food and beverage brands 29% – Cutting back the number of side dishes and desserts 28% – Asking guests to bring a dish 22% – Choosing recipes with fewer or cheaper ingredients 18% – Cutting back on alcohol purchases Consumers who are hosting Thanksgiving say they are removing the following from their menu to decrease spend: 29% – pumpkin pie 29% – corn 29% – sweet potatoes 27% – cranberries 23% – green beans 22% – turkey 22% – stuffing Why are more than half of consumers relying on restaurants for Thanksgiving dinner? In a nutshell, consumers want less stress and more time to have fun. 65% – I just want to enjoy the holiday 40% – I don’t want to deal with the hassle of buying ingredients and cooking 32% – It’s cheaper or costs the same as buying all the ingredients to cook at home 22% – I’m too busy 19% – I’d rather have a professionally cooked meal “Trading in aprons for quality time with guests is fast becoming a modern Thanksgiving tradition,” said Brendan Sweeney, CEO and Co-founder of Popmenu. “Restaurants we work with have already earned $20,000, $50,000 or even $150,000 in Thanksgiving pre-orders. At the same time, you’ll notice cost-cutting at the Thanksgiving table with consumers opting to downsize guest lists or skip some holiday staples.” The following is a sample of restaurants that have already generated well over $10,000 in Thanksgiving pre-orders and counting: Max’s Restaurant (locations across the U.S.) Larsen’s Restaurants (CA) Redwood Smoke Shack (VA) Chef’s Market Cafe & Takeaway (TN) Common Grill (MI) Slow Hand BBQ (CA) Blue’s Egg + Bakery (WI) Survey Methodology Popmenu conducted an anonymous nationwide survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers ages 18 and older from November 17 to November 18, 2026. In a nutshell, consumers want less stress and more time to have fun. 65% – I just want to enjoy the holiday 40% – I don’t want to deal with the hassle of buying ingredients and cooking 32% – It’s cheaper or costs the same as buying all the ingredients to cook at home 22% – I’m too busy 19% – I’d rather have a professionally cooked meal “Trading in aprons for quality time with guests is fast becoming a modern Thanksgiving tradition,” said Brendan Sweeney, CEO and Co-founder of Popmenu. “Restaurants we work with have already earned $20,000, $50,000 or even $150,000 in Thanksgiving pre-orders. At the same time, you’ll notice cost-cutting at the Thanksgiving table with consumers opting to downsize guest lists or skip some holiday staples.” The following is a sample of restaurants that have already generated well over $10,000 in Thanksgiving pre-orders and counting: Max’s Restaurant (locations across the U.S.) Larsen’s Restaurants (CA) Redwood Smoke Shack (VA) Chef’s Market Cafe & Takeaway (TN) Common Grill (MI) Slow Hand BBQ (CA) Blue’s Egg + Bakery (WI) Survey Methodology Popmenu conducted an anonymous nationwide survey of 1,000 U.S. consumers ages 18 and older from November 17 to November 18, 2026. articles.title: How First Watch is Building a Culinary Innovation Pipeline at Scale
articles.titleKo: How First Watch is Building a Culinary Innovation Pipeline at Scale
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . When Shane Schaibly joined First Watch in late January 2014, the brand spread through 15 states with about 115 restaurants. He had graduated at the top of his Johnson & Wales class nine years earlier before spending time at fine-dining brands like The Ritz-Carlton, South Beach, and Tampa’s Café Point before heading to Front Burner Brands’ The Melting Pot in 2007. At the specialty chain, he set the Guinness World Record for World’s Largest Cheese Fondue, rising from manager of culinary development to director of F&B to, ultimately, corporate chef, where he developed items and opened stores around the world. Schaibly’s First Watch career began by directing culinary and LTOs. Chris Tomasso, then CMO (he became CEO in 2018), said at the time: “Shane’s experience and love for creating unique seasonal food will be a fantastic addition to our team.” It’s fair to say neither realized what was quite in store. Twelve years later, First Watch has tacked on some 565 units and more than doubled its state count to 33. But one of Schaibly’s core principles during that span hasn’t changed. He set out to make First Watch’s growth feel controlled, in a sense. The chain’s culinary agility and “follow the sun” approach to ingredients is something few have tried to execute at this scale. There are no microwaves, deep fryers, or heat lamps at any First Watch. “Entrees are made to order,” Schaibly said at the brand’s inaugural investor day in Boston, “not because it’s the easy way, but because it’s the right way. Behind that freshness is a highly intentional operational model, including ingredient cross utilization, low single-use SKUs, and kitchens designed to handle fresh food at high volumes.” “Innovation only works if it can be executed consistently,” he added. RELATED: For First Watch, it’s Been ‘Strategy Set, Results Delivered’ Since Going Public Schaibly’s presentation covered a marriage of what’s changed, and what hasn’t—a theme that threaded throughout the company’s first gathering of investors since going public in 2021. He mentioned the brand believes it’s “the only restaurant of our size that can still do this at scale.” It’s required a 360-degree collaboration to get there, where First Watch’s culinary works alongside other business functions. The chain sources seasonal produce at peak (“follow the sun”) and delivers fresh items three to four times every week at every location. Schaibly said First Watch’s operating foundation offers it latitude to innovate yet also requires discipline. Earlier in 2026, the brand refreshed its core menu for the first time in a decade (it normally runs on a five-year cycle, but COVID got in the way). The new menu arrived February and was designed to strengthen mix, encourage incremental purchases, and create more higher-margin sales opportunities. And naturally, it brought forward over 25 items with 30-plus grams of protein. First Watch’s rolling innovation pipeline works 12–18 months out and starts with 50–60 ideation items. Twelve to 15 are evaluated for two to three months and then five go to about 25 restaurants for 10 weeks before five launch systemwide. So, what’s on holiday menus presently were top of the funnel back in February 2025. Schaibly says the recent push, though, wasn’t “innovation for innovation’s sake.” “We created items that the customers want and that improved the overall economics of the entire menu,” he said. Additionally, First Watch adjusted the color scheme and layout and repositioned some of its top performers and higher-margin items to maximize visibility. It also brought optionality into the fold to ensure guests “could get exactly what they were looking for every single time they dined with us,” Schaibly said. Regarding protein, First Watch, without creating new menu items, was able to go in and identify north of 25 existing products with 30 grams or more.

Huey Magoo’s , the fast-casual brand known for its handcrafted chicken tenders, celebrates the grand opening of its 18th location in Georgia, expanding its presence in the state with a new restaurant in Port Wentworth. Every tender starts with the best 3 percent of the chicken, the tenderloin, and is served hand-breaded, marinated for 24 hours and grilled, or sauced and tossed in buffalo, sweet red chili, lemon pepper or garlic Parmesan. The 2,560-square-foot endcap restaurant features a drive-thru, indoor dining and outdoor seating. Guests can enjoy dine-in service, takeout and online ordering through Huey Magoo’s mobile app and website, as well as delivery through DoorDash and Uber Eats. The restaurant is owned and operated by franchise partners Dawn Zmuda, CEO; Pawel Zmuda, CFO; and Amanda Griffin, operating partner, who bring more than 40 years of combined restaurant industry experience. Port Wentworth marks their fourth Huey Magoo’s location, joining three restaurants they currently operate. “Opening our fourth Huey Magoo’s is an exciting milestone for our team, and we’re looking forward to becoming part of the Port Wentworth community,” said Pawel Zmuda, CFO. “We’ve seen firsthand how much guests appreciate the quality of the food and the variety of options Huey Magoo’s offers. We’re excited to bring that same experience to our newest location.” The menu includes a variety of customizable options, including fresh-made salads, sandwiches, wraps and tender meals. Guests can also enjoy hand-spun chips, freshly prepared coleslaw, banana pudding and house-made specialty dips, including Magoo’s, Spicy Magoo’s and Ranch. Additional signature flavors include buffalo, honey mustard, BBQ, garlic Parmesan, sweet red chili and bleu cheese. Magoo’s Rewards™ loyalty program allows members to earn points toward free food with every purchase. New users receive a buy one, get one free 10-piece Tender Bites meal with a beverage purchase to redeem within 30 days. Members earn 10 points per $1 spent, with catering orders earning one point per $1. The Huey Magoo’s mobile app makes ordering, tracking rewards and accessing exclusive offers convenient. “Seeing franchise partners like Pawel continue to invest in Huey Magoo’s speaks to the strength of our brand and the opportunities for continued growth,” said Mike Sutter, chief operations officer of Huey Magoo’s. “With this being his fourth restaurant, Pawel understands what makes the Huey Magoo’s experience special, from the quality of our chicken tenders to the hospitality our guests expect. We’re excited to introduce Huey Magoo’s to more guests in the Savannah area.” Huey Magoo’s Port Wentworth is now open at 4 Magnolia Blvd., Suite 100, Port Wentworth, GA 31407. The dining room is open daily from 10:30 a.m. to 9 p.m., and the drive-thru is open daily from 10:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. For more information, visit HueyMagoos.com, download Huey Magoo’s mobile app or contact the restaurant at 912-468-5529. articles.title: One Bad Shift is Not a Bad Employee
articles.titleKo: One Bad Shift is Not a Bad Employee
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Picture a Friday night that got away from somebody. Not a disaster. A normal bad night. She’s behind from the jump, she snaps at a cook, a table waits 20 minutes for a refill, and at some point she stops trying to catch up and just survives until close. You watched it happen. And somewhere around 8:30, without intending to, you decided something about her. That’s the part worth sitting with. Nobody announces the verdict. You don’t write it down or say it out loud. You just walk out that night carrying a slightly different opinion of a person than you walked in with, and from then on you lead her like the person you saw on Friday. How a Shift Turns Into a Label What happens next is quiet and it’s fast. You start noticing differently. The next time she’s a little short with somebody, that’s not a bad moment anymore, that’s a pattern. Meanwhile the three solid shifts she worked in between don’t register at all, because nothing happened on them. Good shifts are invisible. That’s what makes them good. Within a month you’ve got a story about her, and the story feels like evidence because you keep finding things that fit it. You’re not making it up. You’re just only counting half the data. Then the story starts making decisions. Who gets the Saturday close. Who trains the new hire. Who gets asked when you need somebody to stay late. Who you think of when a shift lead spot opens up. None of those feel like judgments about Friday. They’re just choices you make without thinking much. And she notices all of them. The Only Things We Write Down Here’s the structural problem underneath all of it, and once you see it you can’t unsee it. Think about what is actually in a team member’s file. A write-up, a corrective action, a documented conversation, maybe a note from the time something went sideways and HR needed a record of it. Now think about what’s not in there. The Tuesday she caught a 10-top walking in at 9:50 and made it work. The month she covered three call-offs without complaining. The new kid she quietly trained because nobody else would. We only document failure. There’s no form for a good Tuesday. So every person you lead has a written record made up entirely of their worst days, and then at review time, or promotion time, or termination time, we open that record and treat it as the story of who they are. It isn’t. It’s a highlight reel of their bottom 5 percent, and we built it that way ourselves. I’ve sat in a lot of rooms where a decision about somebody’s future got made off a folder like that. Nobody in the room was being unfair on purpose. They just had the only evidence anybody ever bothered to create. It Runs the Other Direction, Too This is the part most leaders miss, and it costs more: One great shift doesn’t make a great employee either. We do this constantly. Somebody handles a brutal rush with poise one night, or says exactly the right thing to an angry guest while you happen to be standing there, and that person gets promoted in your head on the spot. Three weeks later they’re a shift lead. Four months later you’re wondering what happened to them, when nothing happened to them. You made the call off one night and the night was not representative. And the good-shift version is harder to catch, because nothing about it feels like a mistake while you’re making it. Writing somebody off at least carries a little guilt. Promoting somebody feels generous. Over 10,000 field visits I’ve watched both versions of this, and the promotion mistake is more expensive than the write-off mistake, because now somebody’s carrying a job they can’t do yet, in front of a team that can tell. It is the same bias running the other way, and nobody calls it a bias when it arrives as a compliment. What Actually Tells You Something A single shift tells you about a shift. articles.title: Giordano’s to Open in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee
articles.titleKo: Giordano’s to Open in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Big things are coming to the Smoky Mountains. Giordano’s, the iconic Chicago pizza brand known for its world-famous stuffed deep-dish pizza, is officially coming to Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, with plans to open one of its largest restaurants at 2050 Parkway in Spring 2027. Known as The 1 for Chicago-Style Pizza , Giordano’s will transform the former Hard Rock Cafe space into a 14,000-square-foot landmark dining destination designed to welcome the millions of travelers who visit the Smoky Mountains region each year. Located between WonderWorks and the future Play District, powered by Hasbro, the restaurant will bring more than 50 years of pizza-making tradition and Chicago hospitality to the heart of Pigeon Forge’s tourism corridor. At the center of the experience will be the authentic stuffed deep-dish pizza that has made Giordano’s a Chicago tradition for generations. The Pigeon Forge restaurant will produce its own fresh, never-frozen dough and make its signature pizza sauce on site. Each pizza will be crafted with Wisconsin mozzarella sourced from local dairy farmers, hand-picked Mendocino County tomatoes, and layers of premium ingredients. Baked inside Giordano’s signature double crust, the pizza delivers the rich, buttery flavor and famous cheese pull that have kept guests coming back for more than 50 years. The restaurant will blend Giordano’s Chicago roots with the distinctive character of Pigeon Forge through custom architectural elements and larger-than-life details inspired by both destinations. The exterior will feature a custom façade showcasing Chicago’s skyline and iconic landmarks, bringing a piece of the Windy City to the Smoky Mountains. Inside, guests will encounter a replica Chicago “L” train car and a large bear installation, a playful nod to the area’s mountain surroundings. “Pigeon Forge is a destination where families come to have fun and make memories, and we could not imagine a better place to go big with the Giordano’s experience,” said Nick Scarpino, CEO of Giordano’s. “My wife, kids, and I have enjoyed visiting Pigeon Forge in the past, so this is a full-circle moment for me, personally. This restaurant will bring together our Chicago heritage and the distinctive energy of the Smoky Mountains, creating a memorable gathering place that feels unmistakably Giordano’s and uniquely Pigeon Forge.” Guests can dig into Giordano’s full menu, featuring its famous stuffed deep-dish pizza, crispy tavern-style pizza, traditional thin-crust pizza, appetizers, salads, sandwiches, desserts, and beverages. The restaurant will offer dine-in, carryout, and delivery, giving residents and visitors multiple ways to enjoy Giordano’s Chicago-style favorites. With its expansive footprint, fresh on-site pizza production, destination-inspired design, and full menu of Chicago favorites, the restaurant is poised to become a must-visit stop for families, friends, and travelers after a day exploring the Great Smoky Mountains and surrounding attractions. “At Smith Global, we are committed to investing in the continued growth and development of Pigeon Forge & Sevier County by bringing quality businesses, exceptional dining destinations, and exciting new opportunities to the market. articles.title: The Chef Who Had to Leave His Kitchen Built the Compliance Platform the Industry Never Had
articles.titleKo: The Chef Who Had to Leave His Kitchen Built the Compliance Platform the Industry Never Had
articles.originalSummary: After a spinal injury ended his career behind the pass, Michael White spent years watching professional kitchens struggle with the same paper-based systems he’d worked under. Chef-Ops-Pro is his answer. Michael White spent the better part of his career in professional kitchens. Then a car accident changed everything. The consequences didn’t appear immediately. It was years later that the full impact became clear — two damaged discs at L4 and L5 of his spine, leaving him without the physical mobility that kitchen life demands. By 2011, after years of progressively moving into management roles as his condition worsened, he left the industry he had built his career in. “You don’t just walk away from kitchens,” says White. “That environment gets into you. The pace, the pressure, the standards you hold yourself to. I didn’t stop thinking like a chef — I just couldn’t stand in one anymore.” What stayed with him, alongside the identity of the industry, was the frustration of how it was run. Temperature logs on clipboards. Compliance records in folders that went missing before inspections. Staff training documented on paper that nobody could find when an EHO officer walked through the door. The same inefficiencies, year after year, in an industry that had digitalised almost everything except its back-of-house operations. While a number of platforms exist that serve portions of this problem — some focused on allergen management, others on temperature logging or HACCP checklists — operators wanting full coverage have typically had to stack multiple disconnected tools. The result is software that cannot cross-reference data between modules, creating the same fragmented picture that paper systems produced, just in digital form. Chef-Ops-Pro is the platform White built to fix that. Launched in June 2026, Chef-Ops-Pro brings together EHO compliance reporting, temperature logging, blast chill records, HACCP checklists, staff training documentation, rota management, food cost tracking, and procurement into a single cloud-based platform — accessible on any device, from any location. Because every module sits within the same platform, data is connected across the operation — giving kitchen managers and operators a complete picture rather than a collection of separate records. “Every other part of a restaurant operation has been modernised,” says White. “Reservations, payments, ordering, marketing — all digital. But the kitchen compliance folder is still sitting on a shelf next to the pass, full of paper that nobody can read and records that go back three weeks at best. That’s the gap I built Chef-Ops-Pro to close.” The platform is designed to serve the full range of UK food businesses — independent restaurants, pub kitchens, hotel F&B operations, care home kitchens, contract caterers, school canteens, and mobile catering operations. Pricing starts at £40 per month for single-site operators, with multi-site pricing from £25 per property per month. For White, the launch is both a business and something more personal — a way back into an industry he never really left. “I built this for the kitchen managers and head chefs who are doing everything right but still spending Sunday night worrying about what an inspector might find on Monday morning. That used to be me. It doesn’t have to be anyone.” A free trial is available at www.chef-ops-pro.com

articles.title: How Naked Farmer is Growing Without Giving Up Ownership
articles.titleKo: How Naked Farmer is Growing Without Giving Up Ownership
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Naked Farmer plans to nearly double in size next year. Naked Farmer founder Jordan Johnson had emptied his life savings into opening his first restaurant when the pandemic brought the industry to a standstill in 2020. The Tampa-based concept was supposed to introduce customers to fresh, locally sourced meals built around relationships with regional farmers. Instead, Johnson found himself with a restaurant he couldn’t open and a business model that suddenly seemed impossible to execute. Then he visited a grocery store. Produce shelves were empty. Meat was scarce. National supply chains had been disrupted, leaving consumers struggling to find basic ingredients. The farmers Johnson had spent the previous year getting to know faced the opposite problem. Their crops were still growing, but the restaurants and farmers markets that purchased them had shut down. Johnson saw an opportunity to connect the two. Within 72 hours, Naked Farmer became a digital farmers market, selling produce boxes, free-range chicken, and grass-fed beef through its website and third-party delivery platforms. The company delivered food directly from local farms to customers before eventually opening its restaurant for takeout and limited dine-in service. The unconventional launch helped Naked Farmer establish relationships with customers and suppliers during one of the industry’s most difficult periods. It also provided an early test of a concept that Johnson believed could extend well outside Tampa. Six years later, Naked Farmer operates 11 restaurants across Florida, North Carolina, and Tennessee, with its 12th location expected to open soon. The company opened five restaurants in 2026 and plans to add another 10 in 2027, nearly doubling its footprint over the next year. The expansion comes with an unusual distinction. Johnson has been able to grow the business without surrendering a significant ownership stake to outside investors. A longstanding relationship with Valley Bank, initially supported by Small Business Administration financing, has played a major role in making that possible. The partnership began when Naked Farmer’s first restaurant demonstrated that its farm-to-table model could attract customers and produce promising financial results. Johnson wanted to expand, but he also wanted to avoid the pressure that can accompany raising equity capital. Valley Bank provided SBA-backed financing that allowed the company to open additional restaurants and establish a track record across multiple locations. The arrangement also imposed financial discipline, requiring each restaurant to demonstrate that it could succeed without a substantial reserve of outside investment. “Each restaurant had to have a compelling unit economics. It had to deliver. We didn’t have the luxury of a ton of cash on the balance sheet. We didn’t have margin. It was like every day mattered,” Johnson says. That scrutiny extended into real estate decisions and restaurant profitability. Naked Farmer’s operating model adds another layer of complexity, with its menu changing six or seven times annually according to the availability of seasonal ingredients from farms throughout the Southeast. Benjamin Powers, Valley Bank’s director of corporate and middle market banking, has known Johnson since college. That personal connection helped establish an initial level of trust, but the bank still needed evidence that Naked Farmer could repay its loans. Powers was familiar with the concept from its early digital farmers market operation and had seen its transition into a restaurant business. The financial results impressed him. The challenge was determining whether those results could be sustained and replicated. Anthony & Luca’s Pizza Kitchen is serving a limited-time GTA VI Special at all three of its locations, adding a new pizza to its lineup of New York, New Jersey, and Philadelphia-inspired favorites. The special arrived in mid-November, timed with the anticipated November 19, 2026, launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The game is set in the fictional Florida-inspired state of Leonida, including Vice City. Anthony & Luca’s operates two Florida locations in Pinellas Park and Tampa, along with a third restaurant in Houston, Texas. The GTA VI Special is an Anthony & Luca’s menu item only and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Rockstar Games. The limited-time pizza features a thin, crispy Jersey Boardwalk-style crust with cheese layered beneath the sauce. It is made with Grande mozzarella and a plum-tomato marinara swirl, then topped with cup-and-char pepperoni, chopped Calabrian hot chili peppers, caramelized onions, and a drizzle of Mike’s Hot Honey. The pizza is available in medium and extra-large sizes. Anthony & Luca’s menu draws inspiration from New York, New Jersey, and Philadelphia. Its hand-stretched, thin-and-crispy New York-style dough is made daily using a three-generation family recipe and New York City water. The menu also features Philadelphia-style cheesesteaks made with more than half a pound of thin-sliced USDA ribeye, sautéed onions, and Cooper Sharp American cheese on a toasted Amoroso roll baked in Philadelphia. Additional offerings include wings, arancini, panzerotti, and Italian street food.
